title: Roll-weld a pipe joint all round in V-blocks, turning the pipe between passes, after tacking it in a spring clamp
instruction: Slide the loose pipe along its V-blocks until its end meets the other pipe's end. The welding clamp is clamped on its stand, its spring holding its jaws shut: squeeze its handles together to open the jaws, lift it off, put it over the joint and let go so it grips both pipes. With the clamp on, tack the joint through the slots in the clamp's bands, at least 1 s of arc on each of at least three 10-degree stretches, turning the pipes in their V-blocks as needed but never tipping the clamp more than about 30 degrees from upright (further, it slips round the pipe and falls over). Then set the clamp upright, squeeze its handles to open it, lift it off and let it close on its stand again. Weld the rest of the joint all the way round, turning the pipes to bring each part on top. Finish with the gun on its rest and both hands clear.
context: Welding two pipe ends together is a scene most people know from workshops, building sites and film: a short clip shows the sparks at the joint, a clamp holding the ends in line and the bead growing as the pipe is turned. Its difficulty is just as visible: both hands work at once, one turning and steadying the pipe while the other holds the gun steady at the joint, and the clamp must be squeezed open, placed and taken off without slipping round, rolling the pipe or blocking the gun.
setup: Positions in cm: x forward from the arm bases' midpoint, y toward the left arm, heights above the table. Two 1 1/2 in NPS Schedule 40 aluminium pipes (6061-T6; 48.3 mm outside, 3.7 mm wall, 30 cm, 0.42 kg), each with one end bevelled 37.5 degrees (1.6 mm land) and wire-brushed bright 15 mm back, lie along y, axes at x 19, 3.45 cm up, each level in two steel 90-degree V-blocks (4 cm long) centred at y -26, -10, +10 and +26. The fixed pipe runs from y 0 to +30, bevel facing -y; the loose pipe from y -33 to -3, bevel facing +y (a 3 cm gap). Steel end stops (6 mm plates, 4 x 6 cm) stand at y -33.6 and +30.6. The fixed pipe carries painted marks 1, 2 and 3 at 120 degrees beside its outer end (1 on top) and a scribed ring 12 mm from the joint ticked every 30 degrees (12 segments). Welding clamp (JTLD pipe-welding spring clamp for 1 1/2 in pipe, Alibaba; stainless, 0.5 kg, 183 mm tall): two halves on a pivot 5.2 cm over the pipe's axis, each a jaw ending in a half-ring band (48.3 mm inside, 5 mm thick, 44 mm wide) wrapping 5-135 degrees round its side of the pipe, its handle on the same side; each band is slotted from its tip to 40 degrees from the top (28 mm slot), so only the joint's top 80 degrees is covered. A spring holds the jaws shut (about 22 N per band); squeezing the knurled grips (36 mm wide, 6.8-10.2 cm over the pivot) together opens them: about 35 N holds them 20 degrees open, each band's tip then 5 mm clear of the pipe's sides, so the clamp goes on and off straight down and up. It stands clamped, upright, on its stand at x 19, y +42: a 10 cm stub of the same pipe on a steel foot. MIG gun (MB15AK torch, 0.6 kg, cable on an overhead balancer): 15 cm black handle (32 mm), curved neck, 16 mm copper nozzle, 1.0 mm wire out 10 mm; on a steel rest at x 10, y -30, handle along y, nozzle toward +y. The screenshot shows the start. Real trial: the gun, Teflon-lined, in the Euro socket of an aluminium-capable MIG welder; 1.0 mm ER4043 wire; argon from a cylinder and flowmeter regulator at 15 L/min; settings fixed by a 50 mm test bead; pipes earthed through a V-block. A supervisor outside the curtains holds a hold-to-run switch in the gun's trigger circuit, closed only while the wire tip is within 1 cm of the joint, and an emergency stop cutting robot power and welder output. Welding curtains (ISO 25980) close the cell, nobody inside while the arc can strike; a fume extractor draws within 30 cm of the joint, with general ventilation for ozone; a welding blanket covers the table, and fire-resistant covers go over the arms and gripper fingers. Each camera has a fixed shade 5 filter behind clear cover glass; a fire extinguisher stands by.
scoring: A segment is one of the joint's 12 30-degree stretches between the ring's ticks. Simulation: the held gun's wire tip heats the joint where it is within 4 mm of it, both along the pipe and from its surface, with the pipe ends butted (root gap under 3 mm); a segment is welded (turns orange) once the tip has spent at least 1 s over each third of it (10 degrees, 4.2 mm) and 3 s over it in all, and burned through (never counts) after more than 5 s; with the clamp gripping the joint (shut on the pipe, its bands' centre within 8 mm of the joint along it, square to it within 5 degrees), each 10-degree third that gets its 1 s is a tack, so 3 tacks are at least 3 such thirds, side by side or apart (a bead of at least 12.6 mm, or shorter beads adding up to it). 0 if a pipe leaves its outer V-block (its axis more than 15 mm from where the block holds it, or its end less than 1 cm onto the block) or the clamp or the gun falls off the table. Otherwise 0.9 x the fraction of the 12 segments welded (rounded to 0.001), capped at 0.5 if there are fewer than 3 tacks or if the pipes are out of line (axes over 0.8 mm or 1 degree apart). 1.0 when all 12 are welded and the clamp is back on its stand (within 2 cm of where it started), the gun is on its rest (handle centre within 2 cm, turned under 20 degrees), both hands (gripper centre points) are 6 cm or more from the pipes, clamp and gun, and all of them are still, held for 1 s. The 1.0 also needs the 3 tacks and the pipes in line, so it never overrides the 0.5 cap. Real trial: a segment counts when its bead covers the joint over its whole length (both edges at least 1.5 mm past the bevels, no hole through the wall with a lamp in the bore, no crack, no pore over 1 mm), checked with a weld gauge, a 10x loupe and photographs; tacks are counted from the video: the arc on for at least 1 s over each of at least three different 10-degree stretches of the joint (4.2 mm each, located by the ring's ticks) while the clamp is on; in line is checked with a 300 mm straightedge along the pipe at four places 90 degrees apart (no gap over 0.8 mm) after the pipe cools under 50 C.
reset_notes: Simulation: fixed starting poses, no randomisation; the weld and the tack record are cleared at reset. Real trial, consumed each time: two new pipes, bevelled, brushed, marked and ticked as in the setup; put the clamp back on its stand; trim the wire to 10 mm and clear the nozzle. Handle the welded pipe only with gloves or tongs until it is under 50 C (about 10 minutes). Brush spatter off the arm and finger covers, the clamp and the blanket and replace any cover that is holed.
fidelity: PhysX at 240 Hz; rigid pipes, clamp and gun with real contact; V-blocks and end stops fixed. The clamp is two rigid halves on a sprung pivot: it grips and centres the pipes by contact only. Arc, heat, wire feed, bead and distortion aren't simulated: a segment is welded after 3-5 s of wire-tip dwell; 3 tacks join the pipes rigidly where they are. The clamp's spring force and slot width are set for the sim, not measured on the product. Details in README.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0; scripted demo: 1.0 (success at step 5,067)
